cards.text: Intracranial arachnoid cysts: about {{c1::1%}} of intracranial masses, M:F {{c2::4:1}}, more often on the {{c3::left}}. Most common site: {{c4::sylvian fissure (≈ 50%)}}, then CPA, supracollicular, vermian and sellar. The only extradural one is the {{c5::intrasellar}} cyst. On MRI an arachnoid cyst follows CSF on all sequences; an epidermoid is {{c6::bright on DWI}}.

zeilen: Small, biconvex, anterior temporal tip, no mass effect; communicates freely on CT cisternogram
Proximal and middle sylvian fissure, open insula (rectangular shape); partial communication
Entire sylvian fissure, marked midline shift, bony expansion of the middle fossa; minimal communication; brain rarely re-expands fully after surgery
cards.notiz: Greenberg Fig. 15.1, p. 261. Treatment options for symptomatic cysts: microsurgical or endoscopic fenestration into the basal cisterns, or cyst–peritoneal shunt.

zeilen: 80% male, palpable keel-like ridge, frontal bossing
Triangular forehead, hypotelorism; associated with 19p chromosomal anomalies
Flat forehead on the affected side, **harlequin eye** (elevated lesser wing on X-ray), amblyopia risk
Short, broad skull; often syndromic (Crouzon, Apert)
Ipsilateral occipital flattening, ear displaced **posteriorly**, trapezoid head shape
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 264–268. Incidence ≈ 0.6/1000 live births; raised ICP in ≈ 11% with a single suture.

cards.rueckseite:
**Positional:** occipital flattening with ipsilateral **frontal bossing** and the ipsilateral ear displaced **anteriorly** → **parallelogram** head (seen from above); improves with repositioning, tummy time, helmet.
**Lambdoid synostosis:** ipsilateral ear displaced **posteriorly**, contralateral parietal bossing → **trapezoid** head; may have a palpable ridge or trough over the suture.
If unsure: reposition and recheck in **6–8 weeks**; positional cases improve.

**Causes:** congenital **forking** (multiple small channels), true narrowing, **septum/web**, periaqueductal **gliosis** (after infection or hemorrhage), **X-linked** (L1CAM, adducted thumbs), external compression (tectal glioma, pineal mass, vein of Galen malformation).
**Imaging:** dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized **fourth ventricle**; sagittal MRI shows the obstruction.
In adults it can present late (LOVA, longstanding overt ventriculomegaly in adults).
**Treatment:** **endoscopic third ventriculostomy** (ideal indication) or shunt.

Maldifferentiation of the meninx primitiva, not a true tumor.
**Location:** ≈ 50% **pericallosal** (interhemispheric), often with **corpus callosum agenesis**; also quadrigeminal cistern, CPA, suprasellar.
**Imaging:** fat density on CT (may have curvilinear calcification), T1 bright, suppressed on fat-sat.
**Treatment:** almost never surgical; vessels and nerves run through it, so resection is dangerous.

cards.vorderseite: Absent septum pellucidum and septo-optic dysplasia
cards.rueckseite:
Absent septum pellucidum alone is rarely of consequence, but look for associated anomalies (schizencephaly, holoprosencephaly, chronic hydrocephalus).
**Septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier):** absent septum + **optic nerve hypoplasia** + **hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction** (growth hormone deficiency, DI) → endocrine work-up.

Skin-covered spinal dysraphism: a **subcutaneous lipoma** passes through a posterior bony/dural defect and attaches to the **dorsal surface of a low, tethered cord**.
**Clinic:** lumbosacral fatty mass (± hemangioma, dimple, hair), progressive **tethered cord** signs (bladder, foot deformity, weakness).
**Treatment:** prophylactic untethering and lipoma debulking is commonly advised before deficits occur; the placode/lipoma interface is never fully removed.

Congenital fusion of **≥ 2 cervical vertebrae** (failure of segmentation, weeks 3–8).
**Triad** (all three in < 50%): **low posterior hairline**, **short neck**, **limited neck motion** (rotation most).
**Associations:** scoliosis (60%), **Sprengel deformity** (25–35%), **unilateral renal agenesis**, deafness (≈ 30%), synkinesis (mirror movements), cardiac anomalies, basilar impression.
Symptoms come from **hypermobile unfused segments** (instability, degeneration), not the fused ones → screen kidneys, heart, hearing; avoid contact sports with high-risk fusion patterns.

cards.vorderseite: Congenital scoliosis: failure of formation vs. segmentation
cards.rueckseite:
- **Failure of formation:** **hemivertebra** (fully segmented hemivertebrae progress most), wedge vertebra
- **Failure of segmentation:** block vertebra, **unilateral unsegmented bar**
- **Worst prognosis:** unilateral unsegmented bar with a **contralateral hemivertebra** (rapid progression → early fusion)

Screen with MRI for intraspinal anomalies (split cord, tethering, syrinx) and with ultrasound for renal anomalies.

zeilen: Syrinx without tonsillar descent; improves after posterior fossa decompression
Tonsillar herniation plus caudal descent of the brainstem (obex below the foramen magnum)
Chiari II features + high cervical/occipital **encephalocele** containing cerebellum; very poor prognosis
Cerebellar **hypoplasia** without herniation (no longer considered a true Chiari)

cards.rueckseite:
Cyst lined by **GI-type (or respiratory) epithelium** from persistence of the **neurenteric canal** (week 3).
**Location:** usually intradural **ventral** to the cord in the **lower cervical/upper thoracic** spine; associated vertebral anomalies (e.g., diastematomyelia), may connect to the GI tract or mediastinum. Rarely intracranial (posterior fossa, anterior to the brainstem/CPA).
**Clinic:** pain, myelopathy, **recurrent meningitis** (fistula).
**Treatment:** complete resection (recurrence after subtotal removal).

cards.text: Neural tube defect prevention: folic acid {{c1::0.4 mg/day}} for all women of childbearing age, {{c2::4 mg/day}} after a previous affected pregnancy. Drug risk factors: {{c3::valproate (1–2%) and carbamazepine}}. Prenatal screening: elevated maternal serum {{c4::α-fetoprotein}} and ultrasound (lemon and banana signs).

zeilen: Midline/bilateral or frontal/occipital masses, diffuse swelling
Decreased alertness, small reactive pupils, Cheyne–Stokes breathing
**Ipsilateral dilated pupil** (CN III) while still awake
Rostrocaudal: diencephalic → midbrain → pons → medulla; decorticate → decerebrate
Rapid coma, contralateral hemiparesis (ipsilateral with Kernohan notch), decerebrate posturing
Pituitary stalk shearing → DI; upward gaze palsy
PCA compression → occipital infarct; Duret hemorrhages

cards.rueckseite:
- **Toxic-metabolic:** **pupils reactive** (even when brainstem reflexes are otherwise depressed), symmetric findings, often asterixis, myoclonus, tremor; fluctuating course
- **Structural:** focal signs, asymmetric pupils/posturing, rostrocaudal progression
- **Exceptions:** fixed pupils with atropine, glutethimide, severe hypothermia, massive barbiturates; pinpoint with opiates and pontine lesions
- **Pseudocoma:** psychogenic (active eye closure, eyes deviate to the ground, normal calorics with nystagmus) vs. locked-in (ventral pons, vertical eye movements preserved)

- Not applicable < **37 weeks** gestational age
- **Two exams**, each **with apnea test**, by **different attendings**, separated by an observation period:
  - term newborn to **30 days: 24 h**
  - **> 30 days to 18 years: 12 h**
- Apnea test: PaCO₂ **≥ 60 mmHg and ≥ 20 mmHg above baseline**
- After CPR or severe injury, wait **≥ 24 h** before the first exam if there are concerns
- Ancillary tests (EEG, flow study) are not required; used if the exam or apnea test cannot be completed, or to shorten the observation period

cards.vorderseite: Management of the brain-dead organ donor
cards.rueckseite:
- **Hypotension** (loss of vasomotor centers + DI): restore euvolemia, **norepinephrine**/phenylephrine, vasopressin
- **Diabetes insipidus:** **vasopressin drip 0.01–0.04 U/min** (preferred, short-acting) or DDAVP 1–2 mcg q 12 h
- **Hypothermia:** warming blanket (also invalidates brain death testing)
- Hormonal support (T4, steroids, insulin) per protocol; correct coagulopathy
- Refer all imminent deaths early to the organ procurement organization

cards.vorderseite: EVD-related infection: definitions and risk factors
cards.rueckseite:
**Incidence ≈ 9.5%.**
- **Contamination:** single positive culture, normal CSF, no symptoms
- **Colonization:** repeated positive cultures, normal CSF, no symptoms
- **Ventriculitis/meningitis:** positive cultures + rising **cell index** or falling CSF:blood glucose (extreme: WBC > 1000/µL, ratio < 0.2) + symptoms

Cell index = (CSF WBC/CSF RBC) ÷ (blood WBC/blood RBC); a rising index is an early sign.
**Risk factors:** duration, **leakage at the site**, **blood in CSF (IVH/SAH)**, irrigation/flushing.
**Organisms:** skin flora (CoNS, S. aureus, C. acnes) and hospital gram-negatives.

**Organisms:** coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae, **Pseudomonas**; pneumococci after skull base/ENT surgery.
**Empiric therapy:** **vancomycin** (trough 15–20) + **cefepime** (or meropenem); severe PCN allergy: aztreonam or ciprofloxacin. Intrathecal (preservative-free) vancomycin/aminoglycoside for severe cases.
Always consider **chemical meningitis**.

Noninfectious meningeal inflammation, typically after **posterior fossa surgery**, IVH, or spillage of **epidermoid/craniopharyngioma** contents (also intrathecal drugs/contrast).
**Onset:** usually **3–7 days** postop.
**CSF:** can look bacterial, but WBC usually < 7500/µL and glucose not < 10 mg/dL; **cultures negative**.
**Treatment:** self-limited; steroids, serial LPs or lumbar drain if protracted; treat the pseudomeningocele.

cards.vorderseite: Recurrent and chronic meningitis: what to look for
cards.rueckseite:
**Recurrent meningitis** → search for an abnormal communication: **dermal sinus** (cranial or spinal), **CSF fistula** (often post-traumatic skull base), **neurenteric cyst**; also immunodeficiency. Mollaret meningitis = recurrent lymphocytic, HSV-2.
**Chronic meningitis:** tuberculosis, fungi, cysticercosis; differential: sarcoidosis, carcinomatous meningitis.

Incidence **0.9–5%**; mostly **S. aureus**. Risk: age, chronic steroids, obesity, diabetes, intraoperative hypothermia; higher with instrumentation.
**Management:** culture, empiric vancomycin + cefepime/meropenem, **debridement** of necrotic tissue and suture material (deep infections in the OR), healing by secondary intention or closure over drains; antibiotics 10–14 days for superficial infection with local care. Instrumentation is usually retained if stable in early infection.

*Nocardia asteroides*: gram-positive, **beaded branching** rods, weakly **acid-fast**, aerobic actinomycete (bacterium, not fungus); inhaled, spreads hematogenously.
**Hosts:** immunocompromised (steroids, transplant, lymphoma/leukemia, AIDS).
≈ 2% of brain abscesses, often **multiloculated**; CNS involvement in one-third of nocardiosis.
**Treatment:** **TMP-SMX + imipenem** (± amikacin), surgery as for other abscesses; therapy for **≥ 1 year**.

Dog tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*; CNS involvement in ≈ 3%.
**Imaging:** large, round, thin-walled cyst with **CSF density**, usually **no enhancement and little edema**, in the white matter; often children; eosinophilia.
**Treatment:** removal of the **intact cyst** (rupture → anaphylaxis and recurrence from scolices): **Dowling technique**, the cyst is floated out by irrigating saline between cyst and brain with the head lowered. Adjuvant **albendazole**.

*Borrelia burgdorferi* (Ixodes tick).
**Classic triad (Bannwarth):** lymphocytic **meningitis**, **cranial neuritis** (especially **facial palsy, often bilateral**), painful **radiculoneuritis**. Late: encephalomyelitis, polyneuropathy.
**Diagnosis:** serology (ELISA + Western blot), CSF pleocytosis with intrathecal antibody production.
**Treatment:** **ceftriaxone** IV or **doxycycline** PO for 14–21 days.
